title: Closing Sesshin Reflection/Birth and Death
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dogen's passage in Genjokoan on firewood and ash, where firewood abides completely as firewood and birth and death include each other. Nomon then tells stories of birth and death from close to home: Mercy, the Kenyan girl Nomon sponsored through school for twenty years, who has just given birth to a son, and two sangha members who recently died. Michael Kalbarer comes to Zen with intense curiosity, receives the precepts two months before his death, and quizzes his doctors about cancer. Edie Norton meets Kobun Chino in a community college class, ordains at seventy-eight, plans her own memorial, and speaks her last words: "Access the light, for this is a solemn moment."

sentences.text: What a wonderful assembly.
Wonderful to see everybody.
And on the screen we have Scott, Kim, [unclear: "Toyle"], Kimberly, and Karen.
And we have many wonderful people here in the hall.
Well, Dogen reflected on birth and death in Genjokoan.
First he noticed that objects seem to change in a way that looks like birth and death.
Firewood becomes ash.
It does not become firewood again.
So we already knew that.
Or did we?
Do we really notice?
And do we understand?
What's happening when you light a fire and put in a piece of firewood?
How can that be?
If you went to science class you could say stuff, but what do you really know?
But then Dogen says, well, even that might not be the whole story.
*Do not suppose that ash is after and firewood before.* And that there is a completeness to every form.
That we should understand that firewood abides in its condition as firewood.
Firewood is completely firewood.
Nothing else but firewood.
Which includes all the potential for everything that did, would, could: tree, water, tree, rain, sun, ash, compost, new tree.
And that birth and death is just like that too.
There's a miraculous process that we don't understand.
That things are born.
People are born.
Everything is born.
Bunnies are born.
Moments are born.
And die.
But don't think that it's this then that.
This includes that.
That includes this.
This is exactly that.
Always and ever.
And the whole text is about this, isn't it?
Things appear to be this way.
Understand that fully.
Investigate fully, he's always saying.
Check it out.
Things have a nature that's bigger than the way they seem to be.
So this is a much nicer condition for me than in our opening practice period sesshin, when I was home with COVID.
And COVID, I forget what number it is, 17 or something.
This little teeny virus that we can't even see.
Millions of deaths.
Birth and death.
Lately it's more obvious to me that I'm surrounded by birth and death all the time.
A few stories about birth and death.
The birth story is connected to death, as they always are.
Another virus, the one that causes HIV AIDS, raged around the world a little earlier: the 70s, 80s, and to this present day.
One of the places that was most powerfully affected, and I don't remember if you know the reason why, was Africa.
Millions and millions of people died.
And a friend of mine, who was actually an early Sangha member, a gay man, had lost his partner to AIDS years before.
He went to a conference in Africa to learn about the effect of AIDS in Africa.
And even though he was a very foreign person going there himself, it broke his heart and changed his life to go to Africa to an AIDS conference.
This is my friend Tim Costello.
One of the people he met was a Kenyan doctor.
He told them that by African standards Kenya has a pretty robust health care system, but there are chronic shortages.
Even basic supplies, they often run out.
Gloves, basic medication.
And Tim, my friend Tim, thought about all the extra medical stuff we have just sitting around everywhere in America.
So he came home.
He started a non-profit called Slum Doctor Program, and he was working full-time for United Way, I think.
Eventually he would get fired for this, but he ran this non-profit from his desk, in spare moments at work.
He had boxes of expired medications under the desk, and gloves, and tape.
And periodically he would send them to the clinic in Kenya.
It just felt like a drop in the bucket to him, but it felt like something he could do.
And then he learned that actually one of the biggest impacts from AIDS in Africa is even bigger than the people who are currently sick.
A much more significant thing for the societies of Africa was the tremendous number of children who have been orphaned.
Millions and millions.
And especially in rural areas, these children are very vulnerable.
Of course, there are good people who have to care for them, but they're vulnerable.
Families are large already.
Resources are limited.
Especially for the orphaned girls, who are likely to end up second or third wives in traditional families, which can be okay, but it can be terrible too, or in prostitution.
And a huge factor that allows those orphaned girls to live healthy, happy lives is education.
Kenya has a strong public educational system actually too, but there are fees.
To us, there wouldn't be much.
A latte a week, maybe.
Maybe a latte a month to go to school.
And you need to buy a uniform.
But if you don't have enough money for a latte a month or a school uniform, your child does not go to school.
And so Tim rebooted his organization to focus on this and to provide scholarships and placements for girls who are AIDS orphans in Kenya.
So much death, and this strong effort from a friend right here in Bellingham, Washington, to help with life.
Then one day I ran into Tim, and maybe he just carried these with him everywhere.
He whips out of his backpack a little folder, which had a picture of this 14-year-old African girl named Mercy Kumu.
And he said to me, "Tim, for $800 a month, you could send this girl to boarding school in rural Africa and cover all her expenses and save her life."
What a ballsy thing to say, right?
And I said, "OK, Tim."
Our child was just about to be finishing preschool and going to public school, and we were paying maybe $400 a month, not a year, for preschool.
So money was going to be freed up, so we did this.
And I ended up sponsoring her and being connected to her for the next 20 years.
I became her dad.
And I went to Africa twice, and the most recent time, to help her get married, I was the father of the bride and walked her down the aisle.
It was a little complicated culturally because my job was to give her to her new husband, like literally.
But that's what they wanted to do, and that's what she wanted.
And this led to a birth.
On January 25th in Nairobi, Kenya, my Kenyan daughter gave birth to a large, healthy baby boy named [unclear: "Berwin Gouel"].
And as it does, that birth was a generator of many amazing changes and challenging changes in her life.
Mercy went on to be very successful at that boarding high school, to earn a bachelor's degree and a master's degree, and has a very good professional job in service.
She works for Save the Children to help other kids in Africa.
And they have much better parental leave laws than we do, actually.
She gets a six-month leave with her new baby.
I haven't gotten to meet my grandchild yet.
Wow.
But we're hoping to fly her here in May or June, so I'll keep you posted.
If you got to meet Mercy around our wedding, maybe you'll get to meet her baby boy.
And how could that be a birth?
This seems a little more like a big deal to us than firewood.
It's the same thing, I guess.
Somehow, everything comes together.
Everything.
How many things have to come together for a baby to emerge?
Unbelievable.
Literally unbelievable.
There was no being.
There is a being.
Or was there no being?
Is there a being?
Dogen would encourage us not to be so sure of anything, but to appreciate the miracle.
And lately, there have been a few new deaths in my life and in the sangha's life, actually.
Early in January, our member and friend Michael Kalbarer died from cancer, in his late 60s, I think.
And then last Tuesday, our long-term member, dear, dear friend, sangha priest Edie Norton died from heart disease.
And basically, she was just, she was done.
Her body and mind were ready to be done.
So tonight, I want to share a few stories about Michael and about Edie.
Birth and death.
These seem to be about two particular people, but of course, they're about all of us.
And they're about every moment of our lives.
Birth and death.
So Michael was an enthusiastic, kind of late arrival to meditation.
A joyful, enthusiastic man.
He had all kinds of background from a varied career: publishing, geology, banking, finance.
And his main quality was an intense curiosity about everything, and a delight in his curiosity.
He was also in long-term recovery from alcohol.
He could talk to you about that in great detail.
He had a trauma history.
And although he was pretty joyful, he had pretty low access to his emotions.
He really didn't know a lot of the time what he was feeling.
These emotional blind spots made relationships with women especially, and with his children, a real challenge for him.
But somehow that didn't get him down.
Maybe that's the blessing of not being sure what you're feeling.
He was accepting: that's how it is.
He moved here in his middle 60s, I think, and in a couple of years I watched him go in and out of three or four or five romantic relationships.
Every time I was like, "Ah, darn, didn't work out."
And the next thing I knew, he was dating again.
He was so happy.
And I knew what was going to happen.
So Michael moved here from Minnesota.
As soon as he got here he had heard about mindfulness, and he wanted to try it out.
Maybe a doctor told him about it.
So he came to one of my early mindfulness stress reduction classes that I used to do.
I'd rent the old Dharma Hall and do them with my other hat on.
And he just loved it.
It was like a new way to be in his mind.
He was always having insights.
He'd stay after class almost every week and tell me about some great new thing he'd realized.
And he was so impressed and excited by the little nonprofit I'd started to offer these mindfulness classes.
He quickly progressed from a dedicated volunteer to a staff person, and then he was on the board of directories, always helping me.
Helping me with organizational stuff, he redid our finances.
He trained Ed Waite, who's also the Red Cedar bookkeeper now, in some advanced bookkeeping.
So part of why Ed is so great is Michael trained him.
For a while he wanted to be kind of a personal assistant to me.
He wanted full access to my schedule, and he wanted to talk to me like every day.
Eventually that got to be too much.
Things were popping up in my schedule.
I didn't know what they were.
And I was kind of like, "I love you, but boundaries.
Get out of my schedule."
But pretty much he loved me.
He loved what I was doing, and he wanted to help.
And he did.
For several years, maybe four or five, he was doing mindfulness with me, and he was kind of circling around the Sangha.
Maybe you didn't know this, but he was kind of circling around the edges of the Sangha.
And it's a little bit like his romantic relationships.
He'd sign up for a Red Cedar event, a sit or a hike, and then something would happen and he'd have to cancel. 100% of the time.
Like 20, 30 times.
Something like that.
So there was some barrier there for him.
I don't know if I never asked or if he actually really didn't know what the barrier was.
But he wanted to practice.
So he'd sign up for something and then cancel.
For a while he even volunteered as registrar.
He worked with Judith Koontz.
You may remember Judith.
They unfortunately were like oil and water.
Oh well.
Two good people that shouldn't be together.
But something shifted eventually.
I can't remember if it was right before his cancer diagnosis or right after.
But somehow the barriers fell away and he could really be a part of the Sangha.
It was mostly the pandemic year, so you might not have seen him much in person, maybe on Zoom.
But he applied himself to Zen in his usual fashion, with intense curiosity, devouring books, asking me and Chris a million questions.
Getting really excited about it.
He went to Chris and then later to me with great enthusiasm, like a great big puppy dog, and said, "Would you be my teacher?"
And of course we said, "Absolutely."
He was just a lovely guy.
But the important thing about this was not that he had more stuff to feed his curiosity.
When he really found Sangha, he found refuge.
He found peace.
He settled down a bit more, a lot more.
And then in what turned out to be the last year of his life, he studied precepts.
He took the class, and Chris and I supported him together and helped him sew rakusu.
I think, Chris, you sewed most of it.
And we gave him a Dharma name: Shu-ho-ho-ken.
And shu-ho is pretty obvious.
It meant study the Dharma.
I didn't see a character in there for curiosity in my little guidebook, but study the Dharma.
And the second two mean phoenix revealed or phoenix arising, coming forth, coming forth.
His jukai ended up being two months before his death.
Of course we didn't know that at the time.
But I was so grateful that that happened while he was alive.
And when he got sick, what did he do?
Of course, he got really curious.
He'd quiz his doctors on every medical detail, having done his homework, and not random internet stuff: getting real books and reading up.
I hope his doctors enjoyed him.
They were asked by him to give little graduate-level seminars at every appointment on the biology of cancer.
And he'd tell me all about this.
I couldn't quite follow it all.
I was in the room, actually, when he had a severe stroke in the course of the progression of the cancer.
It affected his vision.
Suddenly he couldn't see.
I was there when the neurologist came to his hospital room to tell him the neurologist's theory about what had happened.
He was standing there, looking off into space, because he couldn't really see.
He was looking a little bit to one side, not quite on the neurologist's face, but close.
And of course, he was asking all kinds of questions, and really interested.
"Oh, what was it like?
And the shape of the clot."
But of course, we were all subject to change and suffering.
Eventually the cancer was in his brain, and he started having trouble: nightmares, disturbing visions, hallucinations.
His vision half came back and became like a constant hallucination TV show.
On a good day, he'd claim it was really cool.
I don't know if I completely believe him.
And in the last few weeks, he had really frightening nightmares, and he'd wake up unable to really distinguish what was real and what was nightmare.
Perhaps the veil getting thinner.
Another great, surprising blessing of his last couple of years of life was one of those former girlfriends.
He already had an interesting relationship with her.
After they broke up, they ended up being platonic roommates.
That doesn't happen often, I guess.
And then they reconnected in a unique new kind of love relationship that I probably won't understand from the outside.
And they got married.
So in the end, he was married, in a happy, loving relationship.
Dawn saw him through.
She's a strong, grounded woman, with deep care, and she took care of him to the end.
And now she's living on in his place up above Lake Padden.
That was part of why they got married, to make it easier for him to give her his house.
Bless you, Dawn.
There's a line in the Jukai ceremony, when you receive the precepts, that I appreciate deeply.
I got to say that to him when we were about to give him his rakusu, his special Buddhist clothing.
The ceremony says that that garment is to protect you in this life and in lives to come.
As I looked at him, I could really remember more clearly, see more clearly, the part about lives to come, because we didn't know how much longer this life would last.
He told me later he really appreciated that I underlined that.
That was really important to him: that this rakusu was not just for this life, but also for lives to come.
So may you be well in your life to come, wherever that is, Michael, good friend, colleague, student.
What a beautiful and perfectly flawed man you are.
And I'm sure it's perfect right where you are in Nirvana, and really interesting, and you have a lot of questions.
So that's Michael Calbera.
One more story.
Edie Norton's history with us is much longer.
She came to Bellingham, I think in 2004, at the age of 68 or 69, just retired from a varied career in the California Bay Area.
She had been a high school teacher and organizational consultant, and she'd held a variety of administrative roles.
She knew a lot about organizations and teaching and just generally being organized.
I don't know how it is, but Edie just had organizational everything in her genes.
And the amazing thing was she was one of the first people to join the sangha, and now we have many, and some are here.
She joined the sangha already having a deeply established Zen practice.
Such a blessing when somebody comes along.
It's a blessing when people are new, equally.
But it's a special kind of blessing when they come along and they've practiced for a long time already.
I don't remember if there being a sangha here was one of the factors in her choosing Bellingham.
It might have been.
And in fact Edie had been practicing far longer than I had when she arrived.
So she was instantly our most senior member in that way.

I would say a little more about Edie's story, but what I noticed was that it's an interesting challenge to do some storytelling about a Dharma student who has also written their own autobiography in the Dharma.
So I don't know if I have all the details quite right.
Read the book.
Don't believe me.
This is my memory and impression.
I'm not vouching for this to be completely accurate.
All these years I've been watching Norman just make stuff up as he goes along, and so I was starting to do that like I always do.
And then I go, "Uh-oh."
This is a very organized book, of course.
But it's pretty close, I'm sure.
The book is called Autumn Light.
Edie met Zen in a time of crisis, as many of us do.
She had two teenage sons, one from each of two marriages.
She was working full time, trying to raise them.
And her husband was in trouble.
He was a severe alcoholic, deeply depressed, but also a brilliant guy and an academic, who also happened to have a strong interest, an academic interest, in Buddhism and Zen.
But things were not going well, for him, for her, for the family.
You can read about this in detail in her book.
Eventually she was pretty much at the breaking point, and she told him, "Something has to change here."
And they decided they could live on his income, so she could stop working.
And he gave her a book and said, "Why don't you learn about Zen?
That might help you."
So he was the cause of the problem and offering the cure.
He gave her an Alan Watts book, and she was engrossed.
Something clicked, the penny dropped.
And then she was surprised to see a class on Zen Buddhism advertised at the local community college.
So she signed up.
This was maybe 1974, 1975.
I actually grew up in the Bay Area, so it's kind of fun when I hear her story or read it again in the book.
I know all the places.
I know the community college.
I lived in the next town over from where she lives.
So it's all very familiar, like karmically, somehow.
So she goes to the community college, and the instructor enters the room, a Japanese man who she says just danced into the room, or slid into the room.
There was something lively and exciting and yet grounded and just alive, luminous about this man.
And he turned out not to be a religion professor with an academic background in Buddhism or Asian studies.
He turned out to be an actual Zen master.
I never got to meet Chino, Kobun Chino Otagawa myself, so I've heard many stories from his students, including Edie.
He was part of a small group of Japanese Zen priests whom Suzuki Roshi invited over from Japan to help him with this emerging convert Zen movement in California.
Suzuki Roshi could see he needed some help.
So two, three, four priests came over and several of them stayed, including this one, Kobun Chino.
Kobun Chino founded groups all over the place, and he was always in motion himself.
He founded the Santa Cruz Zen Center, where I started regular practice a decade or so later.
He started a mountain retreat center in the Santa Cruz mountains above there called Jikoji.
And he started a sitting group in Los Altos in somebody's house, which is where Edie ended up practicing with a small sangha.
I really can't say all the many ways that Edie's studying with Kobun Chino and the sangha changed her.
The book maybe does a little better.
But it was a critical, life-saving support in a difficult time, and a turning point that would change her life forever.

The second to last time I saw Edie, she said, "I want to show you something," and she went back to her office and brought out a little yellowing piece of paper that she'd put in a plastic sleeve to protect it.
There was writing on there in Japanese, and the lines were flowy and weren't straight.
Someone had tried to follow them with an English translation.
I wish I could remember the exact wording, and I hope I'll be able to find it next time I talk to Dan, her son, who's there now.
It's a note that Kobun Chino wrote to her after her husband died from suicide.
It talked about forgiveness, acceptance, moving on, in just such a beautiful way, and it's been a treasure to her ever since.
There's something in it about understanding her own strength.
So Koban was a wild sort of Zen character.
Most Zen people in Japan are actually pretty much organizational people, very organized, and there's a way you do everything, and the step and the stage, carefully trained and very precise.
And maybe it was some of the wild ones that were like, "America, right on, I'm out of here."
Edie's first Jukai ceremony with Koban happened like this: he showed up at her door one day and said, "Let's do a ceremony."
He brought the rakusu, which probably was machine sewn; maybe he got it from Japan.
They sat down at her coffee table and did a Jukai ceremony.
She barely knew what was going on, but it felt right, felt deeply right.
And Koban gave her the name Shunko Myoko, Shunko Myoko, which means spring light, wonderful happiness.
I think this was not long after her husband's death.
So what confidence he had in her, huh?
And in life and death and rebirth: spring, spring light.
And what confidence he had in the human's ability to heal: wonderful happiness, wonderful happiness.
This was in 1997.
She didn't see a whole lot of him after that.
He drifted off to New Mexico, started his sangha, started sanghas in Europe.
He was all over the place.
And Edie ended up, and I think the sitting group in Los Altos faded away at one point.
Another center started in Mountain View, close by.
I think she didn't relate as much to the teacher there.
So she ended up practicing at Green Gulch.
She'd go up there about once a month for a retreat, a two, three hour drive.
Green Gulch's farm, another place deep in my own practice history as well.
And there she connected with the main teacher there, Tenshin Reb Anderson, and did jukai again with him.
Oh, this time doing it the right way: taking a class, studying the precepts, sewing your own rakusu.
The process takes about a year.
And of course, that's the way we do it here.
I should try the other way, huh?
"Come here, come here, come here.
Your new name is..."
So Reb gave her her second name: Zaren Shingei, Sitting Lotus, Deep Understanding.
This was the year 2000.
Sitting Lotus, Deep Understanding.
That's what he saw.
A couple of years later she moved up here.

When I was getting to know her, even though she was older than me chronologically and in practice, she told me right away she was really happy the sangha was here, that I was here, and that I would be her teacher.
I was surprised and honored by this.
I'm not like Michael, it doesn't occur to me he has questions usually.
I'm like, okay.
So I asked her, "Really?
Why me?"
I remember this to my day.
She said, "Well, I can see you're smart."
That was the first quality.
You're smart.
And she said, "I can see you're determined.
You've created this sangha.
You see things through.
That's what I need.
Someone who sees things through."
She told me early on that she really wanted to figure out how to practice.
Now that she was retired, she had a lot more time and energy, and she really wanted to do this right.
She said, "Well, of course, I'm practicing as a lay person, but how do I do this in a serious way?"
And then I remember her saying that she wanted to be a monk in the world.
But I checked in the book, and the book says I said that.
So probably she's right, not me.
I guess I suggested, "Well, why don't you try to be a monk in the world?
Really take your practice seriously and live in this world."
So we worked on that together.
She worked on it, and I got to talk to her once in a while about it.
One of the challenging things about the monk side of things is that it's a practice of leaving home.
Monks leave.
They let go.
They're released from attachment, especially to family and to home.
And she was in a bit of a crisis about this, actually, already.
Her children were fully grown, and she was having trouble letting go of them.
They were born in this crucible of pain, as a family, with the suicide of her husband.
She had been deeply involved and in constant touch through her children's early adulthood and mid-adulthood.
Now they were, I don't know, late thirties, early forties.
And they were done with mom calling all the time, and emailing and texting and asking them why they don't call enough.
It was very, very upsetting to her.
She didn't get it.
Why aren't they calling me as much?
Of course I loved her deeply, but they were ready for some space.
So she had to practice deeply about this.
It really rocked her to her core, actually.
Who am I if I'm not their mother?
We come to things when we come to them.
So now she's about seventy years old, trying to release a little bit from being a mother.
And she did.
Their relationship healed beautifully, and she ended up being really connected in a healthy way, especially to her granddaughters.
She took the "in the world" part seriously, too.
Not just helping take care of the sangha, but serious volunteering in the community.
She was on the planning commission, on boards of organizations.
Everywhere she went she found slightly messed up organizations, and she would help them straighten up, including ours.
But very gently and very steadily, and she never said anything critical.
It was just, "Oh, you don't have bylaws?
Well, let's write some.
We'll take care of that."
That kind of thing.
She was president of the board, one of our really transformational presidents.
Everyone has been great, but she was kind of amazing in that way.
And then a big shift played out, as it occurred to her and to me that the thing she said early on, "of course I'm a layperson," was that really an "of course"?
Again, I don't remember if I suggested this or she did.
I'll have to check the book.
But somebody suggested that she honor the depth of her practice by not saying "of course I'm a layperson," but "of course I'm a monk, and have been a monk all along."
She ordained in 2013 at the age of seventy-eight.
One of the things we ask our priests to do is to go to Tassajara monastery, because there's this deep monastic root to this whole thing, even though we're not a monastery here.
It's to visit the roots, experientially.
I'm not reading about it like Michael might have.
So we sent her off to the monastery.
Although she lived for eighty-nine years, most of her book here about her life is about these three months.
They were very, very powerful for her.
She was in this rigorous place of practice, trying to be her usual organized, diligent self, doing everything very, very well, and she couldn't.
It was too hard.
The rigorous schedule, waking up at four in the morning or a little before, zazen and work all day, lots of silence, lots of structure.

It's a traditional Japanese monastic practice, which they do a little bit, mostly by accident, at Tassajara: not telling you what you're supposed to be doing and then criticizing you when you do it wrong.
So there's a bit of that going on too.
It was hard on her.
"Why didn't you tell me the way to do it?
Where's the manual?"
Ninety days of this, days and nights.
This is challenging even for young, energetic bodies.
You can imagine in your late seventies how this would be.
Our dear friend Kate took this on in her early seventies, also very challenging.
When I heard how hard this had been, of course I felt kind of guilty: oh shit, I'm sorry.
But actually, no.
It was hard, very hard.
But also valuable, very valuable.
The book is about how this transformed her life yet again.
Returning home, she served our sangha so deeply.
She was so steady.
She was here.
She was open and curious and grounded and organized.
She didn't hold back, but she wasn't loud either.
She was just steady, and so committed.
And you saw her in the last couple of years when she could still get around, sitting in her chair right over there, coming every week, even though it cost her.
That's pretty much all she could do that day, to get down here on Thursday night.
As priests, periodically we put out a call, saying we should do this again, inviting the senior students to mentor the younger students.
Edie would always sign up for that, and all of her mentoring relationships somehow worked out beautifully.
The good thing was that the people she was studying with would come over, have tea, read the next chapter together, and talk about the Dharma in their life with Edie.
That would happen in her house.
In the last years of her teaching with us, she was only in her house, so people could come to her, and they did.
She kept seeing people over tea and Dharma until pretty recently.
Some of those people are in this room, and you'll see them around.
Edie had a deep sweetness, but it was restrained.
She didn't use lovey-dovey language.
When she wanted to tell me she loved me, when I saw her the second to last time, what she said was, "It has been an honor to practice with you."
And I said, "Edie, it's been an honor to practice with you."
And inside I said, I love you so much.
Her last teachings to us were about conscious aging and conscious dying.
She set this out with her usual intelligence and organization and thoughtfulness, to every step of the process.
She aged carefully, consciously, step by step, changing and modifying her routines and choices, prioritizing her wellness, letting go of things when she had to let go of things.
She wasn't always happy about it, and she would indulge sometimes in a little teeny bit of complaining, but then she would move on and let go.
So she wasn't perfect, but she knew how to accept what was happening.
